Two of Jesus' own followers walked seven miles with him, talking about him the whole way.
And they had no idea who he was.
Luke, chapter twenty four.
Sunday. Two disciples leave Jerusalem for a village called Emayus. About seven miles.
One of them is named. Kleeopas.
A stranger falls into step beside them.
Luke tells us exactly who it is. Jesus himself.
But their eyes were holden, that they should not know him.
Holden. Held shut. Not a disguise. Something kept them from seeing.
Art thou only a stranger in Jerusalem?
And then they tell Jesus the story of Jesus.
We trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel.
We trusted. Past tense. Their hope died on Friday.
O fools, and slow of heart to believe.
Beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he walks them through the scriptures.
The greatest Bible study ever given. And Luke doesn't record a single verse of it.
At Emayus, he makes as though he would go further.
Abide with us, they beg. For it is toward evening.
He took bread. Blessed it. Broke it. And gave it to them.
The same four actions from the Last Supper.
And their eyes were opened, and they knew him.
And he vanished out of their sight.
Here is the detail most people miss.
In the Greek Old Testament, nearly the same words, their eyes were opened, appear in Genesis three.
Adam and Eve. Eyes opened to shame.
Here, at another meal, eyes open again. This time to see him.
Did not our heart burn within us, they say.
That same hour, in the dark, they walk seven miles back.
And Kleeopas? The early writer Hejuh-sippus says a man named Clopas was the brother of Joseph.
If that is him, Jesus walked seven miles beside his own uncle. Unrecognized.
They saw him the whole day. They only knew him when he broke the bread.
